title: Making A Large Island
description:
# Making A Large Island

You are given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid`. You may change **at most one** water cell (`0`) into land (`1`).

Return the size of the largest 4-directionally connected island that can exist after performing that operation. If the grid is already all land, return `n * n`.

An island is a group of `1` cells connected only through shared edges, not diagonals.

## Example 1

**Input:** grid = [[1,0],[0,1]]

**Output:** 3

**Explanation:** Flipping either zero connects the two land cells through the new cell.

## Example 2

**Input:** grid = [[1,1],[1,0]]

**Output:** 4

**Explanation:** Flipping the only zero makes every cell part of one island.

## Example 3

**Input:** grid = [[1,1],[1,1]]

**Output:** 4

**Explanation:** No flip is needed; the whole grid is already one island.

## Constraints

* `n == grid.length`
* `n == grid[i].length`
* `1 <= n <= 500`
* `grid[i][j]` is either `0` or `1`.

solutions.name: Separate Label Grid with Iterative DFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the input grid unchanged and write component labels into a separate `color` matrix. First label every existing island and store its area. Then evaluate every water cell by summing the distinct neighboring island colors plus the flipped cell itself.

## Key Insight

A single flip can only connect the islands touching that zero from the four cardinal directions. Distinct component IDs are required because the same island may touch the zero from multiple sides.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Union-Find with Component Sizes
solutions.description:
## Approach

Give every land cell a disjoint-set node and union adjacent land cells. Component roots store island sizes. Each zero cell then collects the unique roots among its four neighbors and sums those component sizes plus one.

## Key Insight

Union-Find separates the connected-component construction from the flip evaluation. After all unions, every zero only needs local neighbor roots, not another flood fill.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2 * alpha(n^2))
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: In-Place BFS Island Coloring
solutions.description:
## Approach

Color each existing island directly in the input grid with labels starting at 2, using BFS to avoid recursion depth. Store each color's area, then scan zeros and merge the distinct neighboring colors.

## Key Insight

The grid values 0 and 1 leave all integers 2 and above free for island IDs. Mutating the grid removes the separate label matrix while keeping the same component invariant.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Land-to-Water Contribution Accumulation
solutions.description:
## Approach

After labeling islands, push each island's area toward adjacent water cells instead of pulling areas from each zero. For every zero, keep the set of component colors that already contributed and a running merged area.

## Key Insight

The best flip can be computed from either side of the boundary. Pushing from land to water makes it explicit that only boundary water cells can beat the all-water baseline.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Row-Run Segment Union-Find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compress every horizontal run of land into one segment ID, then union segments in adjacent rows when they overlap by column. A zero cell checks the segment IDs immediately above, below, left, and right.

## Key Insight

Connected components in a binary matrix can be built by scanline runs instead of individual cells. This reduces the number of disjoint-set nodes on grids with long horizontal islands while preserving exact 4-directional connectivity.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2 * alpha(n^2))
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)
